big_idea: TIME = SECONDS, MINUTES, HOURS. We pick the right unit for the duration.
learning_intention: We are learning to describe duration using the right time unit.
student_learning_goal: I can describe duration using the right time unit.
success_criteria: I can name SECONDS, MINUTES, HOURS.
I can pick the right unit for an event.
I can say that 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Roo and Cal — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Cal: A BLINK = 1 SECOND. Brushing teeth = 2 MINUTES. School day = 6 HOURS! Cal opens: 'SECONDS for the FAST, MINUTES for the MEDIUM, HOURS for the LONG!'
minds_on.teacher_script: Remember Day 3: the ruler told us LENGTH in cm.

steps.instruction: Whole group: pick units for 4 events.
Three stations. A: Sort 16 event cards by unit. B: Time real events with stopwatch. C: Make own event cards.
Stretch at C: estimate before timing.

STRATEGY COMPARE: After Station B, two pairs share HOW they ESTIMATED before timing — Pair A 'Mississippi-counting'; Pair B 'body-pose method'. Class debates which is closer to actual on average. Cite Lehrer (2003) attribute-tool matching.
steps.teacher_prompt: Cal: 'Different paths to estimate. The MATH cares about getting CLOSE to the actual.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at A. Sort obvious cards.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Time physical activities — jumping jacks, running. NO-MATERIALS VERSION: children stand for HOURS (big stretch up), sit for MINUTES (medium pose), and clap for SECONDS (quick). Body becomes the time-unit display.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: names time units; picks right unit; uses 60 rule.

discussion_prompts: How many seconds in a minute?
Cal's preview: tomorrow Roo + Cal join forces — measure ALL attributes (length, mass, capacity, time) at the capstone stations (Lesson 5).
consolidation.exit_routine: Cal's time refrain — 'SECONDS for the FAST, MINUTES for the MEDIUM, HOURS for the LONG!' (3x). Then unit close: 'SMALL unit, BIG count — BIG unit, small count!' Each child records one event timed in the right unit.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says BRUSHING TEETH = 2 SECONDS — repairing the wrong-time-unit trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On time-elapsed work, the trap is unit-of-time confusion: child thinks 'seconds = ANY fast event' or 'minutes = ANY medium event' without anchoring to standard durations. Lehrer (2003) frames this as attribute-tool matching for time. Without anchored time benchmarks, capstone integration cannot ground.

Yesterday Lesson 3 used the ruler for cm. Today the stopwatch reads time in seconds and minutes. Lesson 5 capstones with all 4 measurement attributes.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at A. Card 'brushing teeth'. Child picks SECONDS bucket.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Cal asks — try brushing your teeth as fast as 2 seconds. Let's count: one Mississippi, two Mississippi. DONE!'

Child laughs. 'Right, you couldn't brush in 2 seconds. Brushing takes about 2 MINUTES.'

Guide. 'Cal says — SECONDS = blink, snap. MINUTES = brushing, song. HOURS = school day, sleep.'

If still off: provide a 'time benchmarks' chart with examples per unit.
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child says brushing teeth = 2 seconds: drill physical benchmarks — count '1 Mississippi' = 1 second; '60 Mississippis' = 1 minute; child re-says brushing = ~2 minutes.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can't estimate before timing: model 'I PREDICT this will take ___ seconds' before each timed event; compare prediction vs actual.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child reads stopwatch wrong (minutes:seconds format): drill the colon — 'minutes BEFORE the colon, seconds AFTER.'

parts_outline.task: List 3 events you do at home and pick units.
